items.title: NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in CCG lexicon parser (fromstring) on wide bracket bodies and operator chains
items.description:
## Summary

The public CCG lexicon parser `nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring` parses caller-influenced lexicon text with two pure-Python loops whose cost is quadratic in the input width. A service that parses an untrusted CCG lexicon string can be driven into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU by a few-megabyte input, starving the request worker. No authentication or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

`matchBrackets` consumes a bracket body one character at a time with `inside = inside + rest[0]; rest = rest[1:]`. The `rest = rest[1:]` tail re-slice copies the entire remaining string on every iteration, so a flat bracket body costs O(n^2). `augParseCategory` drives a `while rest != "":` operator loop that re-copies the regular-expression match tail (`rest = app[3]`) once per operator, which is also O(n^2) over a long operator chain. items.title: NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in Tree.chomsky_normal_form right-factor binarization via list.pop(0)
items.description:
## Summary

`Tree.chomsky_normal_form()` binarizes a parse tree and defaults to right factoring. For a node with N children the right-factor branch repeatedly removes the first element of a working list with `list.pop(0)`, which shifts all remaining elements each time, so binarizing one wide node costs O(N^2). An application that converts an attacker-supplied treebank tree to Chomsky Normal Form can be forced into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU by one wide flat tree. No authentication or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

In the default right-factor branch the transform executes `curNode[0:] = [nodeCopy.pop(0), newNode]` inside a loop over the N children of a node. `list.pop(0)` is O(len) because it shifts every remaining element down by one; performed N-2 times over a shrinking length-N list this sums to O(N^2). items.title: NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in ConllCorpusReader SRL instance builder via nested span rescan
items.description:
## Summary

`ConllCorpusReader.srl_instances()` builds semantic-role-labeling instances from a CoNLL corpus block. For a sentence block with P predicates and P span columns, the instance builder rescans every span column (and every span within it) once per predicate while searching for each predicate's head, giving O(P^2 * R) work. A single well-formed block that places the head span in the last column forces the full scan on every predicate, so an application that reads an attacker-supplied CoNLL SRL corpus can be driven into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU. No authentication or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

`_get_srl_instances` iterates over the P predicates of a block; for each predicate it scans every span list and every span within it, using an inner `break` that stops only when a span tagged `V` or `C-V` containing the predicate word is found. When the sole h

items.title: NLTK: BllipParser passes caller-supplied model paths to the bllipparser C extension with no pathsec check, enabling arbitrary read
items.description:
## Summary

`BllipParser` in `nltk/parse/bllip.py` hands caller-supplied filesystem paths to the native `bllipparser` C extension without routing them through NLTK's `pathsec` validation. The constructor parameters `parser_model`, `reranker_features`, and `reranker_weights`, and the alternative `from_unified_model_dir()` entry point, flow directly to the C extension's `load_parser_model()` and `load_reranker_model()` calls, which open and read the given path at the OS level. Any application that passes an attacker-influenced path to this API reads a file of the attacker's choosing from anywhere on the filesystem, outside the NLTK data roots that every other NLTK tool wrapper confines access to.

items.title: ag-psd can exhaust memory when parsing crafted PSD dimensions
items.description:
### Summary
readPsd() commits the image/layer buffers from the declared header geometry (width x height x channels x depth, and per-layer rectangles) before validating those values against the actual data. A tiny crafted PSD declaring huge geometry forces a multi-gigabyte allocation.

### Impact
On ag-psd 30.2.0, Node 24, a 52-byte PSD makes readPsd(buf) commit ~3.17 GB (measured peak RSS) in ~0.45 s before throwing a catchable RangeError ("Offset is outside the bounds of the DataView") — about 61,000,000x amplification. Because the buffer is committed before validation, the allocation OOM-kills the process before the error on essentially any host (uncatchable), and concurrent requests exhaust memory. Any service reading untrusted PSDs with ag-psd is exposed to a remote DoS.

items.title: File Browser: Trailing-slash directory deletion leaves public shares active for recreated paths
items.description:
## Summary

File Browser v2.63.15 can leave a public directory share behind when the shared directory is deleted through a path with a trailing slash. The share cleanup path calls `DeleteWithPathPrefix(file.Path, userID)`, but the Bolt backend performs the database prefix query with the unnormalized argument before trimming the slash for boundary checks. For a stored share at `/a`, deleting `/a/` queries for paths prefixed by `/a/`, so the exact `/a` share is never loaded and never deleted.

If a directory with the same path is later recreated, the stale public share becomes active again and exposes the new directory contents through the old public URL.

items.title: NLTK: Quadratic CPU exhaustion in LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize via unguarded onset reversal loop
items.description:
## Summary

`LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize` in the NLTK tokenizer package contains an unguarded O(n^2) processing loop. When the method is called on a single token that consists of a long run of vowels (for example `"a" * n`), it consumes CPU time proportional to the square of the token length. An attacker who can supply an untrusted token to this public tokenizer API can force a single request to saturate one CPU core for a prolonged period, degrading availability of any service that syllabifies attacker-controlled text. No authentication, special configuration, or user interaction is required.

The method walks the token in reverse and, on every iteration after the first vowel is seen, evaluates the membership test `char_lower + current_onset[::-1] in self.legal_onsets`. The set `legal_onsets` is built by `onset()`, which returns only the characters up to the first

items.title: NLTK: Quadratic CPU exhaustion in TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize via list.pop(0) in quote-restore loop
items.description:
## Summary

`TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize` in the NLTK tokenizer package contains an unguarded O(n^2) processing loop in its quote-restoration step. When the method is invoked on text containing a long run of double-quote characters (for example `'"' * n`), it performs a `list.pop(0)` operation once per quote token, and because `list.pop(0)` is O(length), the total cost grows with the square of the input length. An attacker who can supply untrusted text to this public span-tokenization API can force a single request to saturate one CPU core for a prolonged period, degrading availability. No authentication, special configuration, or user interaction is required.

items.title: NLTK: Unbounded CPU consumption in SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.parse() with ambiguous or self-embedding grammars
items.description:
## Summary

`nltk.parse.recursivedescent.SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.parse()` performs an unbounded top-down search over ambiguous or self-embedding context-free grammars with no wall-clock or step limit. An actor who can influence the grammar and supply a short input to a caller that uses this parser can force a single `parse()` call to pin a CPU core indefinitely, producing a denial of service. The related base class `RecursiveDescentParser` gained a `max_time` wall-clock deadline, but the stepping subclass drives its own step loop and never arms or consults that deadline, and its constructor does not accept a `max_time` parameter, so the guard cannot be enabled on this path.

## Root Cause

`RecursiveDescentParser` bounds its recursive search inside `_parse`: it arms a wall-clock deadline on the first step and raises `TimeoutError` once `max_time` (default 5.0 seconds) is exceeded.

items.title: NLTK: Symlink escape in YCOECorpusReader lets a psd/pos directory symlink read files outside the corpus root within the data sandbox
items.description:
## Summary

`YCOECorpusReader` builds two nested corpus sub-readers whose roots are derived from `self.root.join("psd")` and `self.root.join("pos")` (nltk/corpus/reader/ycoe.py). Because `FileSystemPathPointer.join()` (nltk/data.py) performs a purely lexical containment check and never resolves symlinks, and because `CorpusReader.__init__` (nltk/corpus/reader/api.py) validates a sub-reader root only against the global NLTK data sandbox and not against the enclosing corpus root, a directory symlink named `psd` or `pos` planted inside a YCOE corpus lets the reader anchor its nested sub-readers outside the YCOE corpus root. An attacker who controls the contents of a YCOE corpus loaded under `pathsec.ENFORCE=True` can make `parsed_sents()`, `tagged_words()`, and related methods return file content from other locations inside the allowed data sandbox, defeating the per-corpus-root containment

items.title: Tornado: Open redirect via triple-slash redirect paths
items.description:
### Summary

Due to differences in the way browsers and Python's `urllib` parse urls, browsers treat a string starting with three or more slashes as a protocol-level redirect, while `urllib` does not. This means that the 6.6.0 fix for the RedirectHandler open redirect (CVE-2026-116578, commit cc75ab0e) is incomplete. Tornado 6.6.1 improves the open-redirect detection to handle this case correctly, as well as fixing a regression in the 6.6.0 implementation.

items.title: dnspython has excessive memory and CPU use
items.description:
### Summary

A maliciously crafted zone file could use a WKS record to consume excessive memory and CPU, possibly causing the process to exit due to memory exhaustion.

### Details

The `from_text()` parser does not check that a WKS record service number is between 0 and 65535 inclusive.  It then uses this number to resize the bitmap to accommodate a bit with that offset.  This can cause extremely large memory allocations, and also extends the array very inefficiently, wasting CPU.

### Proof of concept

This demonstrates the failure to limit the service number, though with a value that does not cause excessive memory or CPU consumption.

```
rd = dns.rdata.from_text("IN", "WKS", "10.0.0.1 udp 65536")
```

### Impact

If dnspython is used to read zonefile format where the attacker can control the type and rdata text, the program may consume excessive memory or CPU, denying service.

items.description:
### Summary

`@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http` redacts sensitive URL query parameters on **outgoing (client) spans** but not on **incoming (server) spans**. The server-span path writes the raw query string verbatim into the `url.query` attribute, so credentials embedded in inbound request URLs — AWS presigned-URL signatures, Azure SAS tokens (`sig`), GCS signed-URL signatures — are exported in plaintext to the configured tracing backend.

Configuring the `redactedQueryParams` option **does not change this**, as this applies only to outgoing (client) spans.

### Impact

**Information disclosure / credential leakage** (CWE-200; CWE-532, insertion of sensitive information into telemetry data).

**Who is impacted:** any Node.js service instrumented with `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http` — directly or transitively via `@opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node` — that receives inbound

items.title: AutoMapper: Uncontrolled Recursion with Constructor Parameters
items.description:
### Summary
`MaxDepth`, whether set explicitly or applied by default (64) to self-referential type maps, was not enforced when the recursion goes through constructor parameters. Mapping a deeply nested source to a destination built through its constructor, such as a positional `record`, recurses without bound and throws a `StackOverflowException`. That exception can't be caught and terminates the process. This bypasses the mitigation for CVE-2026-32933.

### Details
The type depth used by `MaxDepth` was incremented only after the destination object was created. Constructor parameters, including child objects of the same type, are mapped while the destination is created, so each level recursed before its parent was counted, and the depth check never tripped.

Affected:
- destination types mapped through constructor parameters, including positional records
- both an explicit `MaxDepth(n)`

items.description:
## Summary

OpenTelemetry Go eagerly materializes W3C baggage metadata into property objects during parsing. Slice growth, serialization, and copying into the internal representation cause **bounded but disproportionate memory-allocation amplification** for a valid, densely populated header. items.title: opentelemetry-go: AttributeValueLengthLimit is fully bypassed by attribute values composed of valid U+FFFD runes
items.description:
## Summary

The `AttributeValueLengthLimit` span/log-record limit can be bypassed entirely with attribute values that consist of valid U+FFFD (REPLACEMENT CHARACTER) runes. The counting-based truncation introduced by the fix for GHSA-p9f8-wvj8-2fg8 (commit `e016a78c9`, first released in v1.33.0) has an "optimistic" fast path that skips every U+FFFD without counting it and without falling back to the correct slow path. A value of 1000 U+FFFD runes (3000 bytes) is stored verbatim even with a limit of 5 characters (15 bytes). The same defect affects the attribute truncation paths in `go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace` (`sdk/internal/attrnorm`), `go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log` (`sdk/log/internal/attrnorm`), and the auto-instrumentation tracer in `go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace` (`trace/auto.go`, introduced in `v1.35.0`).

items.title: sqlite3-ruby: Possible SQL query truncation when a string is 4 GiB or larger
items.description:
### Summary

sqlite3-ruby cast Ruby string lengths (`long`) to `int` before passing them to SQLite. On 64-bit platforms, a string of 4 GiB (2^32 bytes) or larger had its length wrap, so SQLite saw only the first `length mod 2^32` bytes. An attacker who controls the length of a SQL string could truncate the query, for example dropping a trailing `WHERE` clause. The affected paths are:

- the SQL passed to `Database#prepare`, `#execute`, and related methods
- String and Blob values passed to `Statement#bind_param` and related methods
- String and Blob values returned from SQL functions and aggregates defined in Ruby (`Database#create_function`, `#create_aggregate`, and related methods)

sqlite3 v2.10.2 raises `RangeError` when any of these strings is longer than `INT_MAX` bytes.

items.title: AutoMapper: Denial of Service via uncontrolled recursion that bypasses MaxDepth
items.description:
### Summary
The default and explicit `MaxDepth` limits added for CVE-2026-32933 don't apply to several mapping paths. Mapping a deeply nested source through any of them recurses without bound and throws a `StackOverflowException`, which can't be caught and terminates the process.

### Affected paths
- **Polymorphic maps:** derived type maps (`Include` / `IncludeBase`) didn't inherit the base map's `MaxDepth`, and the default limit for self-referential maps was only applied to the base map. A chain of derived objects was mapped without a limit, even with `MaxDepth` set on the base map.
- **Runtime-typed members:** members typed as `object` or an interface aren't seen by self-reference detection, so the default limit isn't applied.
- **Dictionary and dynamic sources:** mapping a nested `Dictionary<string, object>` or `ExpandoObject` (for example, deserialized JSON) onto typed destinations

items.description: ## Summary When a dynamic tag (`const Tag = ...; `) resolves to a string, Astro renders it as a raw HTML element name. The name was filtered to remove characters that could inject attributes, but the filter did not handle `/`. Because HTML parsers treat `/` inside a tag as an attribute separator, a tag name such as `img/src/onerror=alert(1)` was rendered as an `` element with an `onerror` attribute. 'div'; --- hello ``` rendered `?as=img/src/onerror=alert(1)` as live HTML. ## Impact Reflected or stored cross-site scripting, but only in applications that use untrusted input (such as a request parameter or an uncontrolled CMS field) as all or part of an element name. items.title: Astro: Image endpoint in @astrojs/node can read files from a case-variant sibling of the output directory on case-sensitive filesystems
items.description:
## Summary

The `/_image` endpoint used by the `@astrojs/node` adapter checks that a requested local image is inside the build output directory before reading it from disk. That check compared paths case-insensitively. On case-sensitive filesystems (such as Linux), a directory whose path differs from the output directory only by letter case is a different directory, but it passed the check.

For example, with the client output directory at `/srv/app/dist/client/`, a request such as:

```text
/_image?href=/../../DIST/client/secret.png&w=32&f=png
```

resolved to `/srv/app/DIST/client/secret.png` and was served, even though that file is outside the output directory.

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can read image files from outside the output directory, but only when all of the following are true:

- The site uses on-demand rendering with the `@astrojs/node` adapter.

items.description:
### Summary

Nuxt can pick a parent directory that does not declare a workspace as its default `workspaceDir`: the farthest directory with a lockfile when the project is not inside a git repository, or the farthest directory with a `pnpm-workspace.yaml` or `deno.json` file, even one that only holds settings. The Vite dev server allows `/_nuxt/@fs/` requests for any file under `workspaceDir`. A stray lockfile or settings file in a parent directory, such as the home directory, therefore lets anyone who can reach the dev server read files in that directory and everything below it.

### Impact

This affects the development server only; production builds are not affected. All of the following have to hold:

items.title: rails-html-sanitizer: Possible XSS via shared scrubber state in concurrent calls
items.description:
## Summary

`Rails::HTML::SafeListSanitizer` (both the HTML4 and HTML5 variants) shares one `Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber` across every `sanitize` call on the same instance, assigning its `tags` and `attributes` on each call without synchronization. Two concurrent `sanitize` calls with different `tags:` or `attributes:` options can interleave, so one call is scrubbed with the other call's allowlist.

- Versions affected: `< 1.7.2`
- Not affected: none
- Fixed versions: `1.7.2`

## Impact

Action View memoizes a single `SafeListSanitizer` per helper module and uses it for every `sanitize` call in the process, so in a multi-threaded server (for example Puma) all requests share the same `PermitScrubber`. If any code path calls `sanitize` with a more permissive allowlist, an attacker who can trigger that path concurrently with another request can cause the other request to be sanitized with t

items.title: envd: Host file disclosure through requirements path traversal and TOCTOU
items.description:
### Summary

envd’s `install.python_packages(requirements=...)` could read files outside the build context on the host. Content interpreted as dependency entries could appear in build logs and build-step metadata.

Commit f576c92, released in v1.3.5, added path containment validation but left a time-of-check/time-of-use (TOCTOU) race between symlink resolution and opening the requirements file. Commit 9d575b3 addresses this race by opening requirements files through a directory-rooted filesystem handle.

### Details

envd reads requirements files on the host to determine whether their contents can be embedded directly into a pip installation build step.

The vulnerable host-side requirements read was introduced in v0.3.38. Version v1.3.5 added containment checks for static path escapes but remained vulnerable to a TOCTOU race. The complete fix is included in v1.3.6.

items.title: rails-html-sanitizer: Possible regular expression denial of service with certain configurations
items.description:
## Summary

`Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber` restricts the `href` and `xlink:href` attributes of SVG reference elements to local references. That check matched the attribute value against `/^\s*[^#\s].*/m`. In Ruby `^` anchors to every line start and `\s` matches newlines, so an all-whitespace value made the engine rescan the value from each of its line starts, taking time quadratic in its length.

- Versions affected: `>= 1.0.3, < 1.7.2`
- Not affected: `< 1.0.3`
- Fixed versions: `1.7.2`

Only Ruby 3.1 and earlier are affected. Ruby 3.2 added linear-time regexp matching, which makes the pattern linear.

## Impact

An attacker who supplies HTML to be sanitized can consume CPU out of proportion to the input size, by sending an SVG reference element whose `href` or `xlink:href` is a long run of whitespace.

Applications are affected only when the allowed tags are overridden to include an SVG

items.title: OpenTelemetry Python API: Denial of service through quadratic-time traceparent parsing
items.description:
## Summary

`TraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract()` in `opentelemetry-api` is vulnerable to regular expression denial of service (ReDoS) when processing a specially crafted `traceparent` value.

A malformed value containing a trace-context prefix followed by a long whitespace sequence and an embedded newline triggers quadratic-time regex backtracking. Applications that extract trace context from untrusted carriers accepting such strings can experience excessive CPU consumption and request-processing delays.

When extraction runs on an asynchronous server’s event-loop thread, a single malicious message can delay unrelated requests handled by that event loop.

## Exposure conditions

Exploitation requires attacker-controlled input to reach the affected propagator through a carrier that preserves embedded newlines and permits a sufficiently large value.

items.title: Soup Sieve: Exponential ReDoS in selector compilation via \9-run in CSS_ESCAPES/IDENTIFIER
items.description:
### Summary
The IDENTIFIER/CSS_ESCAPES regex (css_parser.py:119-124) exhibits exponential backtracking on a run of ambiguous digit-escapes (`\9`) in an attribute-name or tag position of an otherwise well-formed selector. It fires at compile time (before the SELECTOR_LIMIT guard) via the public `soupsieve.compile()` and BeautifulSoup `.select()`.

### PoC (verified on soupsieve 2.9.2)

    import soupsieve as sv
    sv.compile('[a' + '\\9'*26 + '=x]')   # ~57 bytes -> ~10s; ~16x time per +4 chars

### Novelty
Distinct from the patched GHSA-836r-... (VALUE regex) and GHSA-2wc2-... (comma-list) advisories, which are fixed in 2.9.2; this is a different regex/vector.

### Reachability

items.title: Soup Sieve: Uncontrolled recursion in CSS parser lets nested pseudo-class selectors exhaust the Python call stack
items.description:
## Summary

The Soup Sieve CSS selector parser recurses once per level of nested pseudo-class selector (`:is()`, `:not()`, `:where()`, `:has()`) without any limit on nesting depth. An unauthenticated attacker who can supply a CSS selector string to `soupsieve.compile()`, `soupsieve.select()`, or Beautiful Soup's `soup.select()` / `soup.select_one()` can force the parser to exceed Python's recursion limit with a small crafted input (about 1.6 KB, roughly 330 nesting levels), raising an uncontrolled `RecursionError`. Because this exception is not part of the parser's documented error contract, applications that catch only `ValueError` or `SelectorSyntaxError` see an unexpected failure of the request or task that parsed the selector.

## Root Cause

The parser dispatches each opening pseudo-class token to `parse_pseudo_open`, which calls back into `parse_selectors` to parse the pseudo-class

This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-ffr9-mgrr-wcvr. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

## Original Description
NLTK from 3.2.5 before 3.10.4 contains an algorithmic complexity vulnerability in TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize that allows remote attackers to cause quadratic CPU consumption through repeated list.pop(0) calls. ## Original Description
NLTK before 3.10.4 contains an uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability in SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.parse() that lacks any max_time deadline or step limit. Attackers influencing the grammar can supply an ambiguous self-embedding grammar and short token input to force unbounded top-down search, pinning CPU cores and exhausting worker pools.

items.title: Rucio: Unauthenticated administrator impersonation through SSH challenge tokens
items.description:
## Summary

SSH challenge tokens are mistakenly accepted as valid credentials during the authentication token validation process.

While an SSH challenge token is intended as a short-lived nonce for use in a subsequent SSH key exchange, the function to validate authentication tokens does not differentiate between these and actual authentication tokens. Because challenge tokens are generated based on an account name provided via headers without requiring prior authentication, an unauthenticated attacker can request a valid "challenge" token for any account (including administrative ones) and use it to authenticate against other API endpoints.

## Proof of Concept

items.title: Soup Sieve: Polynomial-time denial of service in the descendant combinator
items.description:
## Summary

Matching a selector that uses the descendant combinator (`a b`) takes time that grows polynomially with how deeply the document is nested, and each extra descendant combinator in the selector raises the degree by one. A selector with `k` descendant combinators takes `O(n^(k+1))` time on a chain of `n` nested elements.

An attacker who controls the HTML or XML that an application passes to Soup Sieve (directly, or through Beautiful Soup's `select()`, `select_one()`, `css.select()`, etc.) can send a very small, deeply nested document that keeps a CPU busy for seconds to minutes against an ordinary selector such as `section div div`.

## Details

items.title: Soup Sieve: General sibling combinator inside :has() matches untrusted HTML in quadratic time
items.description:
## Summary

Matching a selector that puts a general-sibling combinator inside `:has()`, such as `div:has(a ~ b)`, against untrusted HTML runs in O(n²) time in the number of sibling elements. A single small document with a few thousand siblings ties the process up for a minute of CPU, so an application that runs a fixed selector of this shape over HTML it doesn't control can be stalled by one request.

`:has` is powerful, but much in the same way poor regular expressions can be crafted to cause catastrophic backtracking with greedy capturing, has can be used to create non-ideal scenarios that can cause large portions of the tree to be evaluated for one or many elements if not used thoughtfully.

This behavior is not exclusive to Soup Sieve, but browsers make note of these potential performance issues themselves: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Selectors/:has#per

items.title: Active Storage: Possible arbitrary file write and read in image analysis
items.description:
### Impact
A Rails application that processes attachments with ImageMagick may allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on the server and, when attachments are stored with the Disk service, to read arbitrary files readable by the application process. Those files typically include `secret_key_base` and credentials for external systems, which may in turn allow escalation to remote code execution or lateral movement to those systems.

### Details
ImageMagick selects a coder from the content of the file it is given, and some coders act on files named inside the image rather than on the image itself. Active Storage constrained none of ImageMagick's coders, and the ImageMagick analyzer runs when a file is attached, so an attacker who can upload a crafted file may be able to invoke one. Attaching the upload is sufficient; no variant, preview, or `analyze` call is required. One

items.title: Action Pack: Possible DoS vulnerability in Action Controller Live streaming
items.description:
### Impact
`ActionController::Live::Buffer#close` pushes its end-of-stream marker onto the response's bounded queue while it holds the buffer's monitor. When the client has stopped reading and the queue is full, the push blocks, and `Buffer#abort`, which runs when the client disconnects or a write times out, waits indefinitely for the same monitor. Each such response could permanently hold a web server thread and its `ActionController::Live` thread, possibly resulting in a DoS vulnerability through thread exhaustion.

Applications that stream responses with `ActionController::Live`, including `send_stream`, are affected. Applications that serve large files through Active Storage proxy mode are exposed to unauthenticated clients.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

items.title: Action Pack: Possible sensitive session information leak in Active Storage proxy mode
items.description:
### Impact
When `ActionDispatch::Cookies` reads a signed or encrypted cookie that was written under a rotated secret (`config.action_dispatch.cookies_rotations`) or in the format that a `:hybrid` cookie serializer migrates from, it writes the cookie back to the response in the current format, and that write ignores `request.session_options[:skip]`. `ActiveStorage::DisableSession` relies on that option to keep the session cookie off the public, immutable responses of the Active Storage proxy controllers, but those controllers still load the session, so a request carrying an old-format session cookie could receive the rewritten session cookie in `Set-Cookie` on a cacheable response. A shared cache that stores such a response together with its `Set-Cookie` header could then serve one user's session to later requesters of the same URL, or serve an attacker's session to other users.

items.title: Action View: Possible XSS vulnerability in highlight helper
items.description:
### Impact
`ActionView::Helpers::TextHelper#highlight` substitutes each matched phrase into the `:highlighter` string without escaping it and returns the result marked HTML-safe. Because sanitizing leaves quote characters in text unescaped, a match substituted into a quoted attribute value of the highlighter, such as the `<a href="search?q=\1">` form shown in the method's documentation, could end the attribute value and add attributes to the element, possibly leading to XSS. Applications are affected when they pass a `:highlighter` that places a placeholder inside an attribute value and highlight text or phrases that a user controls. The default `<mark>\1</mark>` highlighter and the block form are not affected.

### Details

items.title: Action View: Possible XSS vulnerability in strip_tags
items.description:
### Impact
`strip_tags` in Action View returns its sanitized output marked `html_safe`, but the underlying sanitizer encodes only `&`, `<` and `>`, leaving `"` and `'` unencoded. Because ERB does not escape a string marked `html_safe`, untrusted input passed through `strip_tags` and rendered inside a quoted HTML attribute value could close the attribute and add new attributes, possibly leading to XSS. Applications that render `strip_tags` output from untrusted input inside an HTML attribute, for example in a `title` attribute or a `<meta content>` tag, are affected. Output rendered as element content is not affected.

### Details
`strip_tags` now encodes `"` and `'` in its output, as well as `&`, `<` and `>`, without double-encoding existing entities. Applications that use `strip_tags` output outside HTML, such as in a text template or JSON, now see `"` and `'` where they saw `"

items.title: Action View: Possible XSS vulnerability in text helpers
items.description:
### Impact
With the HTML5 sanitizer (`Rails::HTML5::Sanitizer`, the default vendor on CRuby for applications using `load_defaults 7.1` or later), Nokogiri before 1.19.5 serializes `<` and `>` unescaped inside attribute values. The Action View text helpers `highlight` and `simple_format` sanitize their input and then process the resulting HTML as a string: `highlight` splits it on tag boundaries to insert matches, and `simple_format` splits it into paragraphs on blank lines. An unescaped `>` or a blank line inside an attribute value could cause markup in that value, which the sanitizer left inert, to be emitted as live elements in the helper's `html_safe` output, possibly leading to XSS. Applications that use the HTML5 sanitizer and pass untrusted text to `highlight`, or to `simple_format` with `html_options`, are affected.

### Details
The fixed releases require rails-html-sanitizer 1.7.

items.title: Active Storage: Unsigned Content-Type in GCS direct uploads with cache_control
items.description:
### Impact
When a GCS service is configured with the `cache_control` option, `ActiveStorage::Service::GCSService#url_for_direct_upload` signs direct-upload URLs with V4, and the V4 signature covers only the `Cache-Control` and `Host` headers. A direct-upload client can therefore send a `Content-Type` of its choosing, and can omit the declared `Content-MD5`, without invalidating the URL. GCS stores the supplied content type as object metadata, which takes precedence over the `response-content-type` that Active Storage sets on download URLs, so an uploaded object could be served as inline HTML under the application's bucket path on `storage.googleapis.com`. Script in such an object runs on the storage origin rather than the application's, but could register a Service Worker scoped to the bucket path and read or replace a victim's later responses for signed URLs in that bucket.

items.title: Action Pack: Possible Strong Parameters Bypass in Parameters#each_key
items.description:
### Impact
`ActionController::Parameters#each_key` delegates to the internal `ActiveSupport::HashWithIndifferentAccess` that holds the request parameters, so when called with a block it returns that hash instead of the `Parameters` instance. The hash does not respond to `permitted?`, so Active Model mass assignment (`new`, `assign_attributes`, `update`) accepts it without raising `ActiveModel::ForbiddenAttributesError`. An application that passes the return value of `each_key` to mass assignment could allow a remote, unauthenticated attacker to set attributes that the application does not permit, such as an authorization flag.

This is an incomplete fix of [CVE-2020-8164](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8727-m6gj-mc37), which made `each`, `each_pair` and `each_value` return the `Parameters` instance but left `each_key` delegated.

items.title: Hono: `csrf()` does not check requests sent by hyperlink auditing (`text/ping`)
items.description:
### Summary

`csrf()` validates a request only when its `Content-Type` is one of the three types an HTML form can send. Chromium's hyperlink auditing (`<a ping>`) sends a cross-origin POST with the user's cookies and the content type `text/ping`, which is not in that list. The middleware does not look at `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site` for such a request, so it is passed to the handler.

### Details

The middleware skips the origin check when the content type is not one that a form submission produces. The assumption was that any other content type requires a CORS preflight and therefore cannot be sent cross-origin with credentials. Hyperlink auditing is an exception: Chrome and Edge send the ping as a credentialed POST without a preflight, with a fixed body and `Content-Type: text/ping`.

items.title: Hono: `validator('form')` skips validation for `multipart/form-data` requests with extra parameters
items.description:
### Summary

`validator('form')` only recognizes a `multipart/form-data` `Content-Type` that carries nothing but a single `boundary` parameter. A request with another legal parameter, such as `charset`, or with extra whitespace after the `;` is not recognized as a form. The validation callback then receives an empty object, while `c.req.parseBody()` still parses the body as a form.

### Details

The check that decides whether a request body is a form was written as a strict pattern over the whole `Content-Type` value. Any parameter list that does not look exactly like `; boundary=...` fails the check. When it fails, the middleware does not read the body and passes an empty object to the validation callback. If the callback accepts an empty object, the request proceeds to the handler, which can still read all submitted fields through `c.req.parseBody()` or `c.req.formData()`.

items.title: Hono: `mount()` and `app.mount()` can forward a path that bypasses middleware scoped inside the mount prefix
items.description:
### Summary

`mount()` and `app.mount()` remove the mount prefix from the request path and forward the rest to the mounted application. Two mistakes in that step let a crafted request reach a route of the mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware, such as an authentication check on `/app/admin/*`. The outer application routes on the original path, so the middleware does not run.

### Details

1. **Dynamic prefix** (all affected versions): for a mount such as `/api/:tenant/*`, the prefix was removed by the length of the route pattern, not of the matched prefix. A request with a longer or shorter first segment is cut in the middle, so `/api/a/xxxxx/admin/secret` reaches the mounted application as `/admin/secret`.
2. **Re-normalization** (since 4.12.21): the forwarded path was built from the decoded request path and assigned to `url.pathname`, which

items.title: Hono: RegExpRouter skips wildcard middleware for some route sets and for paths with an encoded line terminator
items.description:
### Summary

RegExpRouter, which the default `SmartRouter` selects for most applications, skipped wildcard middleware in three cases, so a route handler ran without the middleware registered for it:

1. Middleware whose parameter is written with the explicit default pattern, such as `/api/:tenant{[^/]+}/admin/*`, was not applied to a route written as `/api/:tenant/admin/:id`. (since 4.13.0)
2. Middleware on `/admin/*` was not applied to a route registered on `/admin*` for paths under `/admin/`. (since 4.1.4)
3. For a path with an encoded line terminator (`%0A`, `%0D`, `%E2%80%A8`, `%E2%80%A9`), no wildcard pattern matched, so the request reached the not-found handler without any wildcard middleware. (since 4.4.0)

TrieRouter, LinearRouter and PatternRouter apply the middleware in all three cases.

items.title: Hono: `css` helper does not escape a closing tag split between the template and an interpolated value, allowing HTML injection
items.description:
### Summary

The `css` helper in `hono/css` escapes a `/` that follows `<` inside an interpolated value so that a value cannot close the `<style>` element. The check only looks inside each value. When the text before a value ends with `<`, whether that is the template itself or an earlier interpolated value, and the next value starts with `/`, the `/` is not escaped and the combined output contains an unescaped closing tag.

### Details

Interpolated string values are escaped one at a time before they are joined with the surrounding template text. The rule that neutralizes `</` therefore cannot see a `<` that belongs to the template. A template such as a `content` declaration that opens with a literal `<` and interpolates a string right after it produces a raw `</style>` when that string starts with `/style>`. items.title: @grpc/grpc-js: safe_regex incorrectly applies partial string matching for patterns with alternation
items.description:
### Summary

The StringMatcher/PathMatcher for `safe_regex` builds its RE2 as `^${regex}$` with no surrounding group. Because alternation has the lowest precedence, a pattern `"a|b|c"` compiles to `/^a|b|c$/` -- "starts with a" OR "contains b" OR "ends with c" instead of a full match of the whole value. Configurations with `safe_regex` matchers that use a regex alternation (a natural way to list methods or service identities) therefore apply partial string matches. This impacts route selection, xDS credentials, and RBAC.

### Details

`src/matcher.ts`: `SafeRegexValueMatcher` and `PathSafeRegexValueMatcher` both do
```ts
this.targetRegexImpl = new RE2(`^${targetRegex}$`, 'u');
```

and `apply()` returns `targetRegexImpl.test(value)`. With a top-level alternation the anchors bind only to the first/last branch.
